case_analysis.focal_point: Whether economic harms resulting from personal injuries constitute injuries to 'business or property by reason of' a defendant's acts, thereby conferring standing to bring a civil RICO claim under 18 U.S.C. § 1964(c).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1964(c) - Civil RICO standing provision, which grants a private right of action to '[a]ny person injured in his business or property by reason of a violation' of RICO's substantive provisions, requiring both a qualifying injury type and proximate causation.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Medical Marijuana, Inc. and co-petitioners argue that civil RICO standing requires a direct injury to 'business or property' that is distinct and independent from a personal physical injury. They contend that Horn's claimed 'loss of earnings' damages flow derivatively from his personal/bodily injury (THC consumption causing job loss), not from a direct injury to his business or property interests. Allowing such derivative economic claims would improperly expand RICO's scope beyond congressional intent, blur the statutory distinction between personal injury and property/business injury, expose defendants to treble damages and attorney's fees for ordinary tort claims, and create a flood of litigation that transforms personal injury suits into federal RICO actions. Amici supporting petitioners, including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Washington Legal Foundation, Atlantic Legal Foundation, and the U.S. Hemp Roundtable, further warn of severe economic consequences for industries, particularly the hemp sector, if expansive RICO liability is permitted.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Douglas Horn argues that his documented loss of employment and earnings constitutes a cognizable injury to 'business or property' under civil RICO, independent of the characterization of the underlying cause as a personal injury. Horn contends that lost wages and employment-related economic harm are classically recognized forms of property injury under established legal doctrine, and that the statute's plain text does not categorically exclude economic losses that happen to flow from a physical harm. He further argues that the Second Circuit correctly reversed the district court's dismissal, and that imposing an additional requirement that the business or property injury be wholly unconnected to any personal injury would add an 'amorphous' standing barrier not supported by RICO's text or the Supreme Court's precedent in Sedima v. Imrex Co.
key_precedents: Sedima, S.P.R.L. v. Imrex Co., 473 U.S. 479 (1985) - Supreme Court rejected additional 'racketeering injury' standing requirements and emphasized RICO's broad remedial purpose
Holmes v. Securities Investor Protection Corp., 503 U.S. 258 (1992) - Established proximate causation requirement for civil RICO standing under § 1964(c)
Anza v. Ideal Steel Supply Corp., 547 U.S. 451 (2006) - Refined proximate cause analysis requiring direct relationship between injury and predicate RICO act
Hemi Group, LLC v. City of New York, 559 U.S. 1 (2010) - Further narrowed proximate causation under civil RICO
RJR Nabisco, Inc. v. European Community, 579 U.S. 325 (2016) - Addressed scope of civil RICO and standing requirements
Roebuck v. Guttman, 678 F. Supp. 68 (S.D.N.Y. 1988) - Referenced regarding Rule 54(b) certification and judicial economy in the procedural history
Horn v. Medical Marijuana, Inc. (Horn II), 2021 WL 4173195 - District court opinion dismissing the civil RICO claim on legal grounds

Horn v. Medical Marijuana, Inc., 80 F.4th 130 (2d Cir. 2023) - Second Circuit opinion reversing dismissal and holding that economic losses from personal injury can qualify as RICO business or property injury

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor's most refined argument in Round 2 — that Horn's claim is 'structured differently' as a direct claim for employment and wage loss rather than a secondary measure of bodily harm — is the most serious challenge remaining, but I find it ultimately unpersuasive under my minimalist methodology. The structural framing of a complaint cannot determine the substantive legal category of the underlying injury; if it could, plaintiffs could always recharacterize personal injury claims as property claims by pleading economic losses as primary rather than derivative, which would render the § 1964(c) limitation entirely dependent on artful pleading rather than the nature of the harm Congress intended to exclude. I am reinforced in this view by Justice Kagan's observation that Sedima prohibits adding requirements the text omits, not enforcing requirements the text includes — the 'business or property' language is a textual inclusion that must have operative force. As Chief Justice, I would write the majority opinion on the narrowest possible grounds: economic losses that are wholly derivative of and causally inseparable from an antecedent personal physical injury do not independently satisfy § 1964(c)'s 'business or property' requirement, leaving open all questions about economic harms that arise independently of physical injury to the person.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor raises the most compelling counterargument — that lost wages and employment are 'classically recognized forms of property loss' under any ordinary understanding, and that Sedima counsels against erecting additional standing barriers. However, this argument conflates the nature of the injury with the nature of the resulting damages. The critical originalist inquiry is not whether lost wages can constitute property in the abstract, but whether Congress, in 1970, understood 'injured in his business or property' to encompass economic losses that are wholly derivative of and causally inseparable from an antecedent personal bodily injury. The common law tradition at that time — reflected in Black's Law Dictionary and contemporaneous tort doctrine — treated lost wages as parasitic damages flowing from personal injury, not as independent property injuries, and Congress borrowed this framework directly from the Clayton Act. Justice Gorsuch correctly notes that Drake v. B.F. Goodrich and similar contemporaneous decisions confirm this understanding, and permitting Horn's recharacterization would effectively nullify the personal injury exclusion by allowing any bodily harm with economic sequelae to satisfy § 1964(c), transforming RICO into a general federal tort statute with treble damages far beyond what the 1970 Congress contemplated.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor raises the most serious counterargument — that lost wages and employment are 'classically recognized forms of property loss' under any ordinary understanding of the term, and that Sedima counsels against erecting barriers beyond the statutory text. But this argument conflates the nature of the injury with the nature of the resulting damages. The common law distinction, well-established at RICO's 1970 enactment, treated lost wages as parasitic damages flowing from a personal injury — not as independent injuries to property. As Justice Thomas correctly notes, Black's Law Dictionary from that era explicitly distinguished personal injury from property injury, and the 'typical recovery in a personal injury case' included lost wages as derivative components of the personal harm, not as standalone property claims. Justice Sotomayor's reading would effectively nullify the 'business or property' limitation entirely, since virtually every personal injury produces economic downstream effects — a result that cannot be reconciled with Congress's deliberate choice to model § 1964(c) on the Clayton Act's limiting language, nor with the proximate cause refinements in Holmes, Anza, and Hemi Group that consistently resist expanding RICO's reach beyond its textual boundaries.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I have carefully considered Justice Thomas's originalist argument and Justice Kagan's textual analysis, both of which converge on the 'parasitic damages' distinction, and I acknowledge this is the strongest challenge to my position — but I remain unpersuaded that it is dispositive. The common law 'parasitic damages' doctrine describes how courts calculate damages in personal injury suits; it does not establish a categorical rule that economic losses can never constitute independent property injuries when a physical event is in the causal chain. Horn's claim is structurally distinct from a typical personal injury plaintiff seeking lost wages as a component of bodily harm recovery — he is asserting a direct RICO claim for the loss of his employment and earnings as property interests, and the predicate racketeering acts (the fraudulent drug test manipulation) targeted those economic interests specifically, not merely his person. Justice Barrett's argument that 'the injury here is to Horn's person' assumes the conclusion: the RICO predicate acts were directed at his job, not his body, and Sedima's instruction to read § 1964(c) generously rather than erecting barriers counsels against extending the personal injury exclusion to swallow cognizable property claims simply because a physical event was in the causal chain. I write separately to note that the nullification concern my colleagues raise, while serious, proves too much — a rule that any economic loss causally traceable to a physical event is categorically excluded would itself nullify legitimate property injury claims, and the proper limiting principle is proximate cause under Holmes, not categorical exclusion.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor's most refined argument in Round 2 — that Horn's claim is 'structured differently' as a direct claim for employment and wage loss rather than a secondary measure of bodily harm — is the strongest version of the respondent's position, and I want to engage it seriously. But I find it ultimately unpersuasive because the 'structure' of a plaintiff's pleading cannot be the operative test; if it were, every personal injury plaintiff could reframe their lost wages as a standalone property claim and circumvent the limitation entirely, which is precisely the nullification problem I identified in Round 1. Justice Barrett's formulation captures the dispositive point most cleanly: the injury here is to Horn's person — the involuntary ingestion of THC affecting his body — and the economic losses are parasitic consequences of that personal injury regardless of how the complaint characterizes them. The common law backdrop Congress legislated against in 1970 did not permit this kind of recharacterization, and Sedima's instruction to read RICO generously prohibits adding requirements the text omits, not collapsing categorical distinctions the text includes — a distinction Justice Gorsuch correctly identifies as controlling here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor raises the most serious counterargument — that lost wages and employment are classically recognized forms of property loss under ordinary meaning, and that Sedima counsels against erecting additional standing barriers. But this argument conflates the nature of the injury with the nature of the resulting damages. The statutory text asks whether the plaintiff was 'injured in his business or property,' not merely whether the downstream economic consequences of an injury can be characterized as property losses. As Justice Thomas correctly notes, the common law at the time of RICO's 1970 enactment treated lost wages as parasitic damages flowing from bodily harm — they were understood as components of personal injury recovery, not independent property injuries. Justice Sotomayor's reading would effectively nullify the personal injury exclusion entirely, since virtually every bodily harm produces some economic consequence, and Sedima's admonition against extra-textual barriers does not authorize courts to collapse the textual categorical distinction Congress deliberately encoded by modeling § 1964(c) on the Clayton Act.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor raises the most compelling counterargument — that lost wages and employment losses are classically recognized forms of property, and that Sedima counsels against erecting standing barriers beyond the text. But this argument conflates the nature of the injury with the nature of the resulting damages. The common law tradition, well-established at RICO's 1970 enactment, treated lost wages as parasitic damages flowing from a personal injury, not as independent property injuries — a distinction that goes to the very meaning of 'injured in his business or property.' As Justice Thomas correctly notes, Black's Law Dictionary contemporaneous with RICO's enactment explicitly distinguished personal injury from property injury, and the Clayton Act lineage confirmed in Holmes reinforces that Congress understood this distinction when it borrowed the limiting language. Allowing Horn's theory would effectively nullify the personal injury exclusion because virtually every bodily harm produces economic downstream consequences, transforming RICO's treble-damages regime into a general federal tort statute in a manner that undermines both the statute's organized-crime purpose and the workability concerns that animated Anza and Hemi Group.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor's most refined argument in Round 2 — that Horn's claim is 'structured differently' as a direct claim for employment and wage loss rather than a secondary measure of bodily harm — is the most sophisticated challenge to the majority position, and I want to engage it carefully. However, this structural recharacterization cannot do the work she asks of it: the injury/damages distinction is not about how a plaintiff pleads or frames her claim, but about the underlying nature of what was harmed. Horn's body was involuntarily subjected to THC — that is the predicate harm — and his job loss flows causally and inseparably from that bodily event. As Justice Kagan correctly observes, Sedima's instruction to read RICO generously prohibits adding requirements the text omits, not enforcing requirements the text includes, and the 'business or property' limitation is textually present. The nullification problem remains dispositive: accepting Justice Sotomayor's 'direct claim' framing would allow any plaintiff to circumvent the personal injury exclusion simply by artful pleading, pointing to economic consequences while disclaiming the underlying bodily harm — a result that cannot be reconciled with Congress's deliberate adoption of Clayton Act limiting language.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor's argument that Horn's claim is 'structured differently' as a direct claim for employment and wage loss — rather than a secondary measure of bodily harm — is the most intellectually serious challenge remaining, but I find it ultimately unpersuasive because it asks courts to look past the causal structure of the injury to its downstream economic characterization, which is precisely the analytical move the injury/damages distinction forecloses. The question under § 1964(c) is not how the plaintiff frames the damages sought, but whether the predicate injury is to 'business or property' — and when the but-for cause of all economic loss is the involuntary physical alteration of Horn's body, the injury remains personal regardless of how the downstream losses are labeled. Justice Kagan's point about Sedima is dispositive on the methodological question: Sedima prohibits adding requirements the text omits, but it does not authorize collapsing categorical distinctions the text includes, and the 'business or property' limitation is precisely such a distinction. My background as a public defender makes me acutely aware that this holding leaves Horn without a federal treble-damages remedy, but the structural concern that Justice Barrett articulates — that permitting economic recharacterization would render the limitation entirely toothless — reflects a genuine textual constraint that Congress, not this Court, must address if the policy outcome is unjust.

John Roberts.reasoning: The text of § 1964(c) limits civil RICO standing to injuries to 'business or property,' and the historical common law distinction — well-established at the time of RICO's 1970 enactment — treated lost wages and loss of earning capacity as components of personal injury damages, not as independent property injuries. Allowing derivative economic harms flowing from a personal injury to satisfy the 'business or property' requirement would effectively nullify Congress's deliberate exclusion of personal injuries from civil RICO's scope, a result inconsistent with the statute's antitrust-law lineage as recognized in Holmes v. Securities Investor Protection Corp. My minimalist approach counsels that where Congress drew a limiting line — excluding personal injuries from § 1964(c) — courts should not erode that line by permitting plaintiffs to recharacterize personal injury damages as property injuries simply because they are economic in nature, as doing so would expose defendants to treble damages and transform ordinary tort claims into federal RICO actions in a manner Congress did not intend. While Sedima cautioned against judicially grafting additional standing requirements onto RICO, the 'business or property' limitation is textual, not judicial, and enforcing it faithfully is the narrowest and most institutionally sound course.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: As an originalist, I must examine the public meaning of 'injured in his business or property' at the time of RICO's enactment in 1970. Black's Law Dictionary (Rev. 4th ed. 1968) is instructive: a 'personal injury' is explicitly defined as 'a hurt or damage done to a man's person... as distinguished from an injury to his property,' and the 'typical recovery in a personal injury case' under common law expressly included lost wages as parasitic damages flowing from the bodily harm — not as independent property injuries. This common law distinction, well-established at the time Congress enacted § 1964(c), strongly suggests that Congress understood 'business or property' injury to exclude economic losses that are derivative of and causally dependent upon an antecedent personal injury, as confirmed by the Court's recognition in RJR Nabisco that the 'business or property' language is 'restrictive' and excludes 'personal injuries.' Allowing Horn's lost wages claim — which flows entirely from his alleged physical harm from THC ingestion — to constitute a cognizable RICO injury would collapse the statutory distinction Congress deliberately drew, contravening the original public meaning of the provision and improperly expanding civil RICO liability beyond what the text supports.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The plain text of 18 U.S.C. § 1964(c) limits civil RICO standing to persons 'injured in his business or property,' a categorical limitation that, consistent with the common law distinction well-established at RICO's 1970 enactment, excludes personal injuries and their derivative economic consequences. As the research materials confirm, allowing downstream financial losses flowing from bodily harm to qualify as 'business or property' injuries would render the statutory limitation meaningless, since virtually every personal injury produces some economic consequence. The Clayton Act analogy is instructive here — Congress modeled § 1964(c) on antitrust standing provisions that were understood to exclude personal injury claims, and permitting Horn's lost wages theory would transform RICO into a general federal tort statute with treble damages, precisely the kind of litigation explosion that practical consequences analysis counsels against. Sedima's rejection of judicially-imposed standing barriers cuts the other way here — it demands fidelity to the text's actual categorical limitation, not an expansion beyond it.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The plain text of 18 U.S.C. § 1964(c) grants standing to any person injured in their 'business or property,' and Horn's documented loss of employment and earnings constitutes a cognizable property injury under any ordinary understanding of that term. As Sedima made clear, courts should not impose additional standing barriers beyond what the statutory text requires, and the petitioners' proposed rule—that economic losses are categorically excluded when they flow from a physical harm—finds no support in RICO's text or legislative history. The statute's distinction between personal injury and business/property injury goes to the nature of the harm suffered, not to whether a physical predicate event occurred; Horn's lost wages and employment are classically recognized forms of property loss, and denying him standing would leave a vulnerable working person without recourse against what he alleges was deliberate corporate misconduct involving mislabeled products. Allowing this claim also serves RICO's broad remedial purpose of providing private enforcement against organized wrongdoing, consistent with the Court's instruction in Sedima to read the statute's remedial provisions generously rather than erecting judicially-crafted barriers.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The text of § 1964(c) requires injury to 'business or property,' and the historical antecedent — the Clayton Act, upon which Congress modeled civil RICO as confirmed in Holmes v. Securities Investor Protection Corp. — consistently treated lost wages flowing from personal physical harm as components of personal injury damages rather than independent injuries to business or property. The statutory distinction between the type of 'injury' and the resulting 'damages' is a well-established common law and legislative drafting convention: economic consequences of a personal injury do not transform the underlying injury into a business or property injury for standing purposes. Allowing Horn's claim would effectively nullify the 'business or property' limitation, since virtually every personal injury produces some economic downstream effect, thereby converting RICO — with its treble damages and fee-shifting — into a general federal tort statute, a result inconsistent with workable statutory administration and contrary to the proximate cause refinements the Court developed in Anza and Hemi Group. While I take seriously Sedima's admonition against grafting additional standing requirements onto RICO's text, the 'business or property' limitation is not an extra-textual barrier but the statute's own express threshold, and fidelity to that text requires holding that Horn's injury — ingestion of an unwanted substance causing job loss — is a personal injury whose economic sequelae do not independently satisfy § 1964(c).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of 18 U.S.C. § 1964(c) limits civil RICO standing to persons 'injured in his business or property by reason of' a RICO violation — a categorical limitation that, read according to its ordinary meaning at the time of enactment in 1970, distinguished injuries to business or property from personal bodily injuries and their downstream economic consequences. As the research confirms, courts contemporaneous with RICO's enactment and shortly thereafter — including the Sixth Circuit in Drake v. B.F. Goodrich — consistently understood that pecuniary losses flowing derivatively from a personal injury were subsumed within the personal injury category and did not independently constitute 'business or property' injury. Sedima's rejection of judicially-imposed standing barriers cuts both ways: just as courts may not add restrictions the text does not contain, they equally may not expand the statute's plain categorical limitation by allowing personal injury plaintiffs to recharacterize derivative economic losses as independent property injuries. Permitting such an end-run would effectively nullify Congress's deliberate choice to exclude personal injury claims from RICO's treble-damages regime, transforming every products liability case involving economic loss into a federal racketeering action — an outcome inconsistent with the statute's text, its historical context, and the proximate causation principles reinforced in Holmes and Anza.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The statutory text of 18 U.S.C. § 1964(c) requires that a plaintiff be 'injured in his business or property,' which reflects a well-established common law distinction between the injury itself and the resulting damages — a distinction deeply embedded in legal tradition at the time of RICO's enactment in 1970. Just as antitrust law, upon which Congress modeled civil RICO per Holmes v. Securities Investor Protection Corp., 503 U.S. 258 (1992), requires a direct injury to business or property rather than derivative economic losses flowing from personal harm, RICO's standing provision cannot be read to permit plaintiffs to recharacterize personal injury damages like lost wages as independent 'business or property' injuries. Allowing such derivative economic claims to satisfy § 1964(c) would effectively nullify the personal injury exclusion, expose defendants to treble damages for ordinary tort claims, and undermine the practical workability of RICO's standing requirements in a manner inconsistent with this Court's narrowing proximate cause jurisprudence in Anza v. Ideal Steel Supply Corp. and Hemi Group. Judicial restraint and respect for Congress's deliberate structural choice to limit civil RICO standing counsel against the Second Circuit's expansive reading, which would transform virtually any personal injury with economic consequences into a federal RICO action.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: As a textualist and originalist, I begin with the plain meaning of § 1964(c)'s phrase 'injured in his business or property,' which Congress modeled directly on § 4 of the Clayton Act. At the time of RICO's enactment in 1970, courts interpreting the Clayton Act's analogous language consistently distinguished between injuries to business or property interests and personal injuries, treating economic losses derivative of bodily harm as personal injury claims not cognizable under the treble-damages provision. Horn's lost earnings flow directly and derivatively from his personal physical injury—the involuntary ingestion of THC affecting his body—and the economic loss is inseparable from that antecedent personal harm; allowing such claims would effectively nullify the statutory distinction between 'business or property' injury and personal injury that Congress deliberately encoded in the text. While Sedima cautions against grafting additional standing requirements onto RICO, it does not authorize courts to collapse the textual distinction between categories of cognizable injury, and permitting derivative economic losses from personal injuries to qualify would expose defendants to treble damages and attorney's fees in circumstances far beyond what the 1970 Congress contemplated when it borrowed the Clayton Act's limiting language.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: While my background as a public defender and commitment to equal protection makes me sympathetic to Horn's position, the text of § 1964(c) requires injury to 'business or property,' and the historical common law distinction — well-established at the time of RICO's 1970 enactment — treated lost wages and loss of earning capacity as components of personal injury damages, not as independent property interests. The antitrust lineage of civil RICO, confirmed in Holmes v. Securities Investor Protection Corp., reinforces that Congress drew a deliberate line between personal injury and business/property injury, and that line cannot be erased simply because the downstream consequences of a bodily harm are economic in nature. Sedima's rejection of additional standing barriers does not compel us to collapse the threshold textual requirement that the injury itself — not merely the resulting damages — be to business or property. Permitting Horn's claim would effectively allow any personal injury plaintiff to reframe lost wages as a RICO property injury, transforming the statute far beyond its organized-crime-infiltration purpose and creating the very litigation explosion that proximate cause doctrines in Anza and Hemi Group were designed to prevent.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether economic harms resulting from personal injuries constitute injuries to 'business or property by reason of' a defendant's acts, thereby conferring standing to bring a civil RICO claim under 18 U.S.C. § 1964(c).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1964(c) - Civil RICO standing provision, which grants a private right of action to '[a]ny person injured in his business or property by reason of a violation' of RICO's substantive prohibitions, along with the broader Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO), 18 U.S.C. §§ 1961-1968.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Medical Marijuana, Inc., Dixie Holdings LLC, and Red Dice Holdings LLC) argue that civil RICO standing requires a direct injury to 'business or property,' and that purely derivative economic losses flowing from a personal physical injury — such as lost wages or loss of employment — do not qualify as cognizable RICO injuries. They contend that allowing such claims would improperly transform personal injury tort suits into federal RICO actions, dramatically expanding civil RICO liability beyond Congressional intent, creating significant litigation abuse, and exposing businesses to treble damages and attorney's fees for what are fundamentally personal injury claims. They further argue that the Second Circuit's ruling conflicts with the majority of circuit courts and established Supreme Court precedent limiting RICO's civil reach.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent Douglas J. Horn argues that his loss of employment and earnings — suffered after he was allegedly deceived into consuming a CBD product that contained THC, causing him to fail a drug test and lose his commercial truck driving job — constitute cognizable injuries to 'business or property' under civil RICO. Horn contends that lost wages and employment-related economic harms are distinct, concrete injuries to his business interests and livelihood, separate and apart from any personal physical injury, and therefore satisfy RICO's standing requirements. He relies on the Second Circuit's ruling affirming that such economic losses are recoverable under § 1964(c) regardless of whether they were proximately caused by conduct that also resulted in personal injury.
key_precedents: Sedima, S.P.R.L. v. Imrex Co., 473 U.S. 479 (1985) — foundational Supreme Court case rejecting additional 'racketeering injury' requirements for RICO standing and broadly interpreting § 1964(c)
Holmes v. Securities Investor Protection Corp., 503 U.S. 258 (1992) — established proximate causation requirement for civil RICO standing under § 1964(c)
Anza v. Ideal Steel Supply Corp., 547 U.S. 451 (2006) — further refined proximate cause analysis for civil RICO claims
Hemi Group, LLC v. City of New York, 559 U.S. 1 (2010) — addressed directness requirement in RICO proximate causation
RJR Nabisco, Inc. v. European Community, 579 U.S. 325 (2016) — clarified scope and extraterritorial application of civil RICO
Horn v. Medical Marijuana, Inc., 80 F.4th 130 (2d Cir. 2023) — Second Circuit decision under review, holding that Horn's lost wages constituted injury to 'business or property' under RICO
Roebuck v. Guttman, 678 F. Supp. 68 (S.D.N.Y. 1988) — cited in lower court proceedings regarding Rule 54(b) certification standards

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Jackson's argument that we are conflating the nature of the injury with the nature of the damages remains the most intellectually serious challenge to my position, and I want to engage with it directly: the difficulty is that her 'analytically separable' framework, however elegant, would apply with equal force to virtually every employed personal injury plaintiff, since one can always describe lost wages as a distinct economic harm to 'business' interests separate from the bodily harm itself. As Justice Barrett correctly identifies, the Clayton Act lineage — which Congress deliberately incorporated — has never permitted this severability maneuver, and Reiter v. Sonotone's 'restrictive significance' language confirms that 'business or property' was understood to carry limiting force excluding derivative economic losses from personal injuries. I remain persuaded that the narrowest defensible holding focuses specifically on the derivative/antecedent personal injury question: where the causal chain runs through a personal injury (involuntary ingestion → failed drug test → job loss), the downstream economic loss does not independently satisfy 'business or property' regardless of how it is characterized, but we need not decide whether fraud directed specifically and exclusively at commercial relationships without any personal injury component would present a different case — preserving that question for another day serves institutional legitimacy while resolving this one on firm textual and historical grounds.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson raise the most serious challenge — that Sedima broadly rejected judicially-imposed limitations on civil RICO standing and that 'business' in its ordinary meaning encompasses employment and livelihood. But this argument conflates the threshold question of what kind of *injury* qualifies under § 1964(c) with the separate question of what 'business' means as a noun. The statute asks whether the plaintiff was 'injured in his business or property' — not merely whether he suffered economic loss. As Justice Barrett correctly notes, the Clayton Act lineage establishes that economic losses derivative of personal injuries remain personal injury damages regardless of how they are characterized, and Congress is presumed to have adopted that settled construction when it borrowed identical language. Justice Jackson's argument that Horn's job loss is 'analytically separable' from his bodily harm proves too much — virtually every employed personal injury plaintiff could make the same claim, effectively nullifying the 'business or property' limitation and exposing defendants to treble damages in ordinary tort cases, a result Holmes and Anza's proximate cause framework was designed to prevent.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the most compelling case for the respondent, arguing that Horn's job loss constitutes a discrete, concrete injury to 'business' in its ordinary meaning, and that Sedima cautions against judicially-imposed limitations lacking textual grounding. However, this argument conflates the nature of the injury with the nature of the damages — the text asks whether the plaintiff was 'injured in his business or property,' not merely whether economic losses resulted. As Justice Kagan correctly observes, Horn's core harm was ingesting an unwanted substance, a quintessential personal injury, and the downstream economic consequences cannot be recharacterized as freestanding business injuries without effectively nullifying the limitation Congress deliberately imported from the Clayton Act. The Clayton Act lineage is decisive for me as a textualist: when Congress borrows language with an established judicial construction — as Justice Barrett emphasizes — we presume Congress adopted that construction, and decades of Clayton Act jurisprudence consistently excluded derivative economic losses from personal injuries, meaning Horn's lost wages remain personal injury damages regardless of how artfully they are pleaded as 'business' harm.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett's Clayton Act lineage argument remains the most formidable challenge to my position, and I acknowledge its force — the presumption that Congress adopts established judicial constructions when borrowing statutory language is a serious methodological constraint. However, I cannot accept that this presumption is conclusive here for two reasons: first, as Justice Jackson correctly identifies, the petitioners' argument conflates the nature of the injury with the nature of the damages, and Horn's injury to his commercial livelihood as a trucker is analytically distinct from any personal injury even if both flow from the same predicate acts; second, the Clayton Act cases the majority relies upon involved plaintiffs whose primary cognizable harm was bodily, with economic loss as a secondary consequence, whereas here the fraud was specifically directed at Horn's employment relationship — the deception targeted his commercial activity as its proximate object, not his body. Justice Kagan's workability concern is real, but the proximate cause requirement from Holmes already does the filtering work she fears is absent, and I would not create a categorical exclusion that leaves workers whose primary economic asset is their labor capacity without RICO recourse against fraudulent enterprises that specifically target their livelihoods. I maintain my position as a dissent, recognizing that a well-reasoned minority view on a close statutory question serves the Court's long-term jurisprudential development.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Jackson's argument that we are conflating the nature of the injury with the nature of the damages remains the most intellectually serious challenge, and I want to engage it directly: the distinction she draws between Horn's 'business injury' (loss of trucking livelihood) and any 'personal injury' (involuntary ingestion) is analytically coherent in isolation, but it cannot bear the weight she places on it because the causal chain is not separable in the legally relevant sense — the predicate RICO acts caused personal injury first, and the economic loss flows through that personal injury, not around it. Justice Sotomayor's invocation of Holmes and Anza's proximate cause framework to do the filtering work is appealing, but proximate cause addresses a different question than whether the injury is to 'business or property' at all; these are sequential gatekeeping requirements, not substitutes for one another. The Clayton Act lineage, as Justice Barrett articulates with precision, establishes that Congress in 1970 imported a settled construction that treated derivative economic losses from personal injuries as personal injury damages regardless of their economic character — and Reiter v. Sonotone's recognition that 'business' has independent meaning does not disturb this, because Reiter involved a plaintiff whose primary injury was to her commercial purchasing activity, not a plaintiff whose primary injury was bodily and whose economic losses were downstream consequences. Accepting Justice Jackson's severability theory would mean that virtually every employed tort victim — anyone whose 'primary economic asset is their labor capacity,' to use her framing — could satisfy the 'business or property' requirement, effectively transforming civil RICO into a general federal tort statute with treble damages, a workability concern that pragmatic statutory interpretation cannot ignore.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Jackson's argument about analytical separability — that Horn's injury to his commercial trucking livelihood is distinct from any personal injury even if both flow from the same predicate acts — is the most intellectually serious challenge to my position, and I want to engage it directly. The flaw, as I see it, is that 'analytically separable' is doing enormous work that the text cannot support: the causal chain here runs Horn's bodily integrity → failed drug test → termination, meaning the business harm is not merely coincident with the personal injury but is causally downstream of it. Justice Barrett's point about the Clayton Act presumption is decisive for me as a textualist: when Congress in 1970 borrowed 'injured in his business or property' verbatim from the Clayton Act, it imported the settled judicial construction that derivative economic losses flowing through personal injury remain personal injury damages, regardless of how artfully characterized. Justice Jackson's concern about leaving working people without recourse is genuinely sympathetic, but the answer to that policy concern lies with Congress, not with this Court rewriting a statutory limitation that has a clear historical meaning — and the proximate cause framework from Holmes already ensures that truly independent business injuries receive RICO protection.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the most compelling case for the respondent, arguing that Horn's job loss constitutes a discrete, concrete injury to his 'business' interests analytically separable from any bodily harm, and that Sedima counsels against judicially-imposed barriers lacking textual grounding. However, this argument proves too much — virtually every employed personal injury plaintiff suffers economic losses 'analytically separable' from their physical harm in the sense that one can describe them in economic terms, yet the Clayton Act lineage that Congress deliberately incorporated into § 1964(c) has consistently refused to permit such recharacterization. As Justice Barrett correctly notes, where Congress borrows statutory language with an established judicial construction, we presume Congress adopted that construction, and the settled Clayton Act rule excluding derivative economic losses from personal injuries cannot be circumvented by pointing to the economic character of the downstream harm. The proximate cause framework from Holmes reinforces this conclusion: the direct injury here was personal and physical, and permitting treble damages under RICO for derivative wage losses would transform the statute into a general federal tort remedy Congress never intended, raising the workability concerns that have guided this Court's consistent cabining of civil RICO's reach.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson raise the most compelling counterargument — that 'business' in § 1964(c) should be read according to its ordinary meaning to encompass employment and livelihood, and that Sedima counsels against judicially-imposed limitations lacking textual grounding. However, this argument proves too much: Sedima addressed whether courts could require a 'racketeering injury' beyond what the text specified, not whether the 'business or property' language itself carries limiting force. The ordinary meaning argument ignores the critical methodological point that when Congress borrows statutory language with an established judicial construction — here, the Clayton Act's 'injured in his business or property' — we presume Congress adopted that construction, including the consistent exclusion of derivative economic losses from personal injuries. Justice Jackson's observation that Horn's job loss is 'analytically separable' from bodily harm is textually creative but practically untenable: the causal chain runs directly through the personal injury (involuntary THC ingestion → failed drug test → job loss), and accepting this severability theory would allow any plaintiff to circumvent the personal injury exclusion by pointing to downstream economic consequences, effectively nullifying the limiting function Congress deliberately built into § 1964(c) as confirmed by J. Truett Payne and the Holmes proximate cause framework.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett's Clayton Act lineage argument remains the strongest challenge to my position, and I acknowledge its force — the presumption that Congress adopts established judicial constructions when borrowing statutory language is a serious methodological constraint. However, I cannot accept that this presumption is conclusive here for two reasons: first, as Justice Sotomayor correctly notes, Reiter v. Sonotone itself gave 'business' an independent meaning that encompasses commercial livelihood, suggesting the Clayton Act's own construction was not uniformly restrictive; and second, the majority's framing consistently collapses the distinction between the *nature* of the injury and the *causal chain* producing it — Horn's commercial trucking livelihood was the direct target of the fraudulent scheme, not merely incidental collateral damage flowing through a personal injury. Justice Kagan's workability concern is serious, but the proximate cause requirement from Holmes and Anza already performs the filtering function she fears is absent, and the majority's categorical rule would leave workers whose primary economic asset is their labor capacity without RICO recourse against enterprises that specifically target their employment relationships through fraud. I maintain my position because the majority's rule creates exactly the kind of atextual categorical exclusion Sedima condemned — one based not on what was injured but on what else was also injured — and that result is neither compelled by the text nor consistent with the statute's remedial purposes.

John Roberts.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 1964(c) limits civil RICO standing to injuries to 'business or property,' language borrowed from § 4 of the Clayton Act, which courts have consistently interpreted to exclude personal injury claims. While Sedima broadly interpreted RICO standing, it did not address whether economic losses derivative of personal physical injuries — such as lost wages flowing from a failed drug test caused by bodily harm — qualify as independent 'business or property' injuries. The most textually and historically defensible reading, consistent with the Clayton Act lineage recognized in Holmes v. Securities Investor Protection Corp., is that Congress drew a deliberate line excluding personal injury and its derivative economic consequences, lest every personal injury tort with an economic dimension become a federal RICO claim carrying treble damages and attorney's fees. Institutional legitimacy and the canon of narrow construction of statutes with severe consequences counsel against the Second Circuit's expansive reading, which would effectively swallow the personal injury exclusion whenever a plaintiff can characterize lost wages as a freestanding 'business' harm.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: As an originalist, I must examine the ordinary public meaning of 'injured in his business or property' as understood when RICO was enacted in 1970. The statutory text of 18 U.S.C. § 1964(c) expressly limits civil RICO standing to injuries to 'business or property,' and at common law and in analogous antitrust contexts, this language was understood to exclude consequential economic losses flowing from personal physical injuries — such as lost wages resulting from an inability to work after bodily harm. Congress modeled § 1964(c) on the Clayton Act's civil antitrust provision, which courts consistently interpreted to exclude personal injury claims and their derivative economic consequences, meaning lost employment income caused by a personal injury (here, involuntary THC ingestion) is properly characterized as a personal injury damage, not an independent injury to 'business or property.' Allowing such claims would also conflict with Holmes v. Securities Investor Protection Corp.'s proximate cause requirement, as the direct injury here was personal/physical, with economic loss being merely derivative — precisely the kind of attenuated causal chain Holmes and Anza cautioned against.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist, I read § 1964(c)'s requirement of injury to 'business or property' as deliberately excluding personal injuries, following the well-established common law distinction that existed at RICO's enactment in 1970. Congress modeled civil RICO on the Clayton Act, which courts have consistently interpreted to bar recovery for personal injury damages, and the research confirms that numerous federal statutes draw the same line between 'injury' and resulting 'damages' — meaning economic losses flowing from a personal injury are still personal injury damages, not independent property injuries. Horn's lost wages and employment losses are quintessential damages derivative of a personal injury (ingesting a substance that harmed him physically and caused him to fail a drug test), not freestanding injuries to his 'business or property' within the meaning of § 1964(c). Allowing such claims would effectively nullify Congress's deliberate exclusion of personal injuries from civil RICO, expose defendants to treble damages for ordinary tort claims, and contradict the majority of circuits that have adopted the antecedent-personal-injury bar.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Sedima's broad reading of § 1964(c), courts should not impose additional barriers to standing beyond what the statutory text requires, and the text's use of 'business or property' — as the Second Circuit correctly recognized drawing on Reiter v. Sonotone — gives 'business' its independent ordinary meaning encompassing employment and livelihood. Horn's loss of his commercial truck driving job and wages constitutes a direct, concrete injury to his 'business' interests as that term was understood at the time of RICO's codification, not merely a derivative consequence of personal injury — the economic harm to his employment is analytically distinct even if the causal chain runs through conduct that also affected him physically. The petitioners' position would effectively create an exclusionary rule that Congress never wrote into the statute, and as Sedima warned, courts should not engraft limitations onto civil RICO that dilute its remedial reach beyond what the text supports. Practically speaking, accepting petitioners' argument would leave vulnerable working people like Horn — deceived by fraudulent commercial conduct into losing their livelihoods — without recourse under a statute specifically designed to address predatory enterprise behavior, a result inconsistent with RICO's broad remedial purposes.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The text of § 1964(c) requires injury to 'business or property,' and careful statutory analysis — informed by the Clayton Act model Congress deliberately adopted — compels the conclusion that lost wages flowing from a personal injury are damages consequential to that injury, not independent injuries to business or property. Sedima broadly interpreted RICO's reach but did not eliminate the threshold requirement that the injury itself be to business or property rather than to person; Horn's core harm was ingesting an unwanted substance, a quintessential personal injury, and the economic consequences downstream cannot be recharacterized as freestanding property injuries without effectively nullifying the 'business or property' limitation entirely. The workability concern is decisive here: permitting plaintiffs to convert any personal injury into a RICO claim by pointing to attendant lost wages or medical expenses would expose defendants to treble damages and attorney's fees in virtually every tort case involving an employed plaintiff, a result Congress plainly did not intend when it cabined civil RICO standing to business or property injuries. The Clayton Act parallel is particularly instructive — antitrust law has consistently refused to allow economic consequences of personal injuries to satisfy the 'business or property' requirement, and there is no sound textual or purposive reason to read RICO's materially identical language more expansively.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: As a textualist, I must begin with the plain meaning of 'injured in his business or property' as it would have been understood when Congress enacted RICO in 1970, drawing on the Clayton Act's identical language from 15 U.S.C. § 15. The historical common law background of that antecedent provision consistently distinguished between injuries to business or property interests — which were cognizable — and personal injuries along with their derivative economic consequences, including lost wages flowing from physical harm. While the Second Circuit's plain-meaning analysis has surface appeal, it elides a critical distinction: Horn's lost employment was not an independent injury to a business interest but rather a downstream economic consequence of a personal injury (involuntary THC ingestion causing a failed drug test), and the Clayton Act lineage of § 1964(c) counsels that such derivative losses were not within the provision's scope. Allowing purely derivative economic losses from personal injuries to qualify would, as Holmes v. Securities Investor Protection Corp. and the proximate cause doctrine suggest, improperly expand civil RICO's reach far beyond what Congress contemplated, transforming every personal injury tort with economic consequences into a federal treble-damages RICO claim — a result the rule of lenity and separation of powers concerns about judicial expansion of private rights of action counsel against.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The statutory text of § 1964(c) limits civil RICO standing to persons 'injured in his business or property,' and this categorical language, rooted in common law distinctions between business torts and personal injury claims, does not naturally encompass derivative economic losses flowing from bodily harm. As this Court emphasized in Holmes v. Securities Investor Protection Corp. and refined in Anza v. Ideal Steel Supply Corp., civil RICO requires a direct connection between the predicate racketeering acts and the cognizable injury to business or property — Horn's lost wages are proximately caused by his personal physical injury (THC ingestion and its bodily effects), not directly by the alleged fraud itself. Permitting such derivative economic claims would effectively transform civil RICO into a general federal tort statute with treble damages, a result inconsistent with Congressional intent and the practical workability concerns this Court has consistently invoked to cabin RICO's civil reach in cases like Hemi Group and RJR Nabisco. Judicial restraint and institutional considerations counsel against expanding RICO liability in ways that would invite mass tort and product liability litigation into federal court under a racketeering framework Congress designed for economic predation, not personal injury suits.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Beginning with the text of § 1964(c), Congress deliberately modeled the civil RICO standing provision on the Clayton Act's identical 'injured in his business or property' language, and as this Court recognized in Reiter v. Sonotone Corp., 442 U.S. 330 (1979), that phrase carries 'restrictive significance' that excludes personal injuries and, critically, economic damages flowing therefrom. The original public meaning of 'business or property' at the time of RICO's 1970 enactment must be understood against the backdrop of decades of Clayton Act jurisprudence, in which federal courts consistently held that economic losses derivative of personal injuries — such as lost wages — do not constitute injuries to 'business or property' but rather remain personal injury damages in different clothing. Allowing Horn's lost-employment claim to proceed would permit plaintiffs to circumvent the personal injury exclusion through artful pleading, transforming what is fundamentally a personal injury tort into a federal RICO action with treble damages and attorney's fees — an outcome inconsistent with the limiting function Congress intended 'business or property' to perform, as confirmed by J. Truett Payne Co. v. Chrysler Motors Corp., 451 U.S. 557 (1981). Methodological consistency demands that where Congress borrows statutory language with an established judicial construction, courts presume Congress adopted that construction, and the Second Circuit's contrary ruling disrupts the settled parallel interpretation of these twin provisions.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The text of § 1964(c) requires injury to 'business or property,' and Horn's loss of employment and wages constitutes a concrete, proprietary economic harm that falls squarely within the ordinary meaning of 'business' as an 'employment, occupation, or profession engaged in for gain or livelihood,' as recognized in the Second Circuit's analysis drawing on Black's Law Dictionary and Reiter v. Sonotone Corp. Sedima broadly rejected judicially-imposed limitations on civil RICO standing that lack textual grounding, and creating a categorical rule that excludes all economic harms merely because they are causally downstream from conduct that also caused personal injury would impose precisely the kind of atextual barrier Sedima condemned. The critical distinction is not whether personal injury was also suffered, but whether the plaintiff can identify a discrete, concrete injury to business or property that is directly and proximately caused by the RICO violation — Horn's job loss satisfies that standard as an injury analytically separable from any bodily harm. My background as a public defender reinforces my concern that restricting RICO standing here would disproportionately disadvantage working-class plaintiffs whose most significant economic asset is their livelihood, effectively immunizing fraudulent enterprises from civil accountability when their victims happen to also suffer physical consequences.
